author: Wajd
title: CPJ outraged by Egypt court conviction of journalist Lina Attalah, order of Mada Masr’s closure
content:
The Committee to Protect Journalists condemns the conviction of Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr, on charges of running an unlicensed website, and calls on Egyptian authorities to reverse the ruling, release the journalist immediately, and end their escalating campaign against independent journalism.

Mada Masr, among the first and few of Egypt’s independent media outlets, and a vital source of critical reporting, has long faced pressure from Egyptian authorities over its journalism. The outlet reported on Tuesday that the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court fined Attalah 3 million Egyptian pounds (about US$54,000), ordered the closure of the outlet, and the confiscation of its equipment. Attalah was subsequently taken into custody, and two Egyptian lawyers confirmed to CPJ that she will remain in custody until the fine is paid.

“The conviction of Lina Attalah and the order to shut down Mada Masr represent a devastating blow to press freedom in Egypt and a direct message aimed at dismantling independent media in the country,” said CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah. “Attalah and Mada Masr are among the most prominent voices in Egypt’s independent media landscape, providing critical reporting on issues of public interest that might otherwise go unreported. author: Amina Khan
title: EU transforms Frontex into a high-tech deportation command centre
content:
Yesterday, 27 October 2026, the European Commission tabled a new Regulation for Frontex, the EU’s border agency, expanding its powers and refocusing its mandate on deportations, preventing arrivals, and surveillance beyond EU territories and into social media. This would effectively turn Frontex into the EU’s deportation agency, equivalent of ICE in the United States.

At the centre of this reform is a budget that would almost double to nearly €12 billion for 2028–2034, leading to a massive expansion of the EU security and surveillance industrial complex. Frontex will test and deploy new technology to repress migrants, funnelling billions of taxpayer money to surveillance, security and defence contractors. EU’s hostile border security regime has for years produced systemic and massive human rights violations of migrants, refugees and racialised people, and those who stand in solidarity with them. This proposal will accelerate that.

Frontex as an ICE-style deportation enforcement agency

The proposal operationalises the recently adopted Deportations Regulation and deepens Frontex’s position as the central actor of a Europe-wide deportation machine. This will make the agency responsible for collecting and analysing data from Member States in order to “predict” deportation needs, and allocating resources to them. Frontex will now have a “Deportation Coordination Centre” that is expected to act at all stages of the deportation procedure, from detecting and identifying people that may be expulsed, booking or arranging flights and escorts, to monitoring their “reintegration” in the destination country.

Alarmingly, it expands Frontex’s powers to deport outside of the EU’s borders. Based on a simple status agreement, Frontex will be able to deport people from one third country to another, with the aim of preventing people from even reaching the EU. This will likely mean sharing sensitive data with third countries and countries of origin, where individuals may be at risk of persecution or harm.

The Frontex mandate reform comes in a package with a proposal to digitalise the management of deportation cases. The border control agency is given a key role in the harmonised technical design of EU and national digital systems, to exchange data on deportations, including sensitive data transfers to third countries (biometric data, travel documents and history, grounds for deportation, health data, etc.), and automate certain steps of the procedure, such as adding deportation orders in the Schengen Information System (SIS) to detect people.

Increased data processing and content policing

With this reform, Frontex’s practice of “debriefing interviews” is codified, particularly during the screening procedure introduced by the Migration Pact. The agency conducts these covert “voluntary” interrogations of people immediately after they disembark or cross the border. During these interviews, the agency extracts data from migrants deemed to be “suspects” of “cross-border crime”, without the possibility for migrants to seek legal counsel. Debriefing interviews have been rightfully criticised for their absence of fundamental rights monitoring and their unfairness as they take place when a person is detained and lacks privacy.

A new “Online Monitoring and Response Centre” will also surveil social media platforms to identify “suspicious behaviours or trends” in people’s movements at the EU borders, and before that, in the countries of origin and transit. Aggregated data collected online will be fed into Frontex’s “risk analysis” to guide border forces’ deployment and reaction. Social media monitoring was already declared as carrying high-risk for violating the fundamental rights of people affected, and was banned by the European Data Protection Supervisor in 2019 when first implemented by the EU Agency for Asylum.

Frontex will also seek designation as a trusted flagger under the Digital Services Act (DSA), allowing the agency to report pieces of online content to platforms for removal, effectively giving the agency extrajudicial powers to police the internet. It may also recommend national authorities to issue binding take-down notices. Frontex depriving people from finding legal support, sharing their stories or expressing solidarity is undoubtedly a serious infringement of freedom of expression.

All information collected during debriefings and online monitoring activities will contribute to Frontex’s border surveillance intelligence gathering called “European situational picture”. It may be combined with data from EUROSUR, Frontex’s information exchange framework with national border authorities, whose scope has been extended to include personal data in supposedly “exceptional” cases. Very sensitive data such as facial images, age, gender, physical and mental state may be processed to provide “situational awareness in situations posing imminent threat to the integrity of the external borders”. This could mean that individuals can be identified and targeted through cross-checking with OSINT data or AI-based identification tools like facial recognition.

Closer cooperation with Europol to further criminalise migration

Under the pretence of fighting the “facilitation of migration”, Europol, the EU’s policing agency, will be able to routinely consult personal data collected by Frontex. This could lead to individuals involved in border crossings, as survivors or supporters, to mistakenly fall under the investigation of Europol possibly with serious consequences, including impacts on their access to legal stay, detention, deportation or even criminal charges.

Quick Reaction Force for illegal pushbacks

Frontex will now also be able to deploy a “Quick Reaction Force”, to react ”flexibly” to “crisis and emergency situations” at EU borders. In this case, flexibility means outside of the usual controls and safeguards. Rather than coordinating humanitarian responses and triggering the solidarity mechanisms Member States agreed upon in the Migration Pact, the Reaction Force will likely aim to quickly and violently deport and force out people who are arriving to seek protection.

Migration repression becomes a market for arms and tech companies

The reform explicitly gives Frontex powers to research, test, and procure new technologies, including AI-enabled tools, drones, sensors and digital analytics. The agency will now be able to run trials, validate products and then procure them at scale, acting in some cases as a central purchasing body for Member States to pool technical equipment, while supplying non-EU countries with more repressive tools. This will reinforce global business for digital surveillance tech and arms, making migration repression a market of its own. The use of such technologies aims to prevent people from even reaching the EU, further outsourcing EU’s responsibility for border deaths and fundamental rights violations to private security companies and non-EU governments.

Protect Not Surveil says: Defund Frontex and resource care instead

The Commission frames migration as a “hybrid threat”, “instrumentalisation” and “weaponisation”, citing events such as Ceuta in 2026 to justify emergency powers and the expansion of Frontex’s surveillance capacities. This dangerous framing conflates individuals as security threats and removes their agency in their decision to move.

For decades, European governments and the EU have responded to migration not by addressing inequality, conflict, climate change, or the reasons people move, but by expanding a militarised border regime. Europe does not need a deportation agency. It does not need ICE. It needs a different approach to human movement: one that recognises movement as a human reality, protects people’s rights, and invests in safety, solidarity and community rather than deterrence and control.

The choice is between a Europe that responds to challenges through militarisation and exclusion, and one that responds through dignity, care, and shared responsibility.

Chloé Berthélémy, Senior Policy Advisor, EDRi, says, “With the new Frontex reform, the EU seems committed to making its borders even more deadly than they already are for people who come seeking safety and protection. The Commission has given a massive boost to the shady surveillance practices of Frontex by doubling their budget and loosening the already-lax data protection rules. The newly introduced social media surveillance, secret interrogations at borders, AI-powered sensors collecting data in real-time will all equip Fortess Europe for illegal pushbacks, more surveillance, and more misery.”

Pauline Fritz, Research and Advocacy Coordinator at the Border Violence Monitoring Network: “The Frontex regulation announced yesterday shows that impunity pays. Not only is Frontex able to receive new powers and a massive funding boost to expand its border surveillance apparatus, it can do so with full immunity for human rights violations and pushbacks that have and will continue to happen under its watch. It is deeply concerning how far the Commission is prepared to go to stop people from reaching safety and building a life in Europe.”

Sarah Chander, Director of Equinox Initiative for Racial Justice, says, “In the most substantial reform of Frontex to date, the EU transforms the agency into the central operations room for its deportation regime, with broader surveillance powers complemented by a bigger standing army.

Doubling Frontex’s budget to bolster kidnappings, prisons and ICE-like systems comes at a time when Europe’s social systems are failing. The EU is cynically distracting us from the real problems – cost of living, failure of social services and the climate crisis.”

Caterina Rodelli, EU Policy Analyst at Access Now, says “The new Frontex reform builds on years of unchecked privileged relationship between Frontex and the arms and tech companies , as in the case of Frontex Industry Days, which gave the private sector abundant face time to pitch their products and set the Agency’s priorities. Frontex will enable big profits from deadly deportation regime.”

Chiara Catelli, Advocacy Officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, says, “This proposal massively expands Frontex’s powers to track, control and deport undocumented people, from inside the EU to third countries and between third countries, without introducing stronger human rights safeguards. All this for an agency with a track record of allegations of complicity in fundamental rights violations.

Deportation operations and immigration detention centres in the EU are already rife with abuse, and we fear that expanding Frontex’s role will exacerbate these abuses within the EU and extend them beyond its borders. This proposal reflects a political obsession with deportations that ignores the realities of migration and Europe’s own economies.”

Emma Musty, Project Coordinator at I Have Rights, says. “At least 12 lives were lost in two shipwrecks last week and in both cases the Hellenic Coast Guards, who deploy Frontex Assets, were involved. Frontex clearly fails its human rights monitoring obligations when such incidents are so prevalent. We are deeply concerned that Frontex’s Mandate could be expanded, when what is actually needed is adequate search and rescue, accountability and safe routes.”

author: Access Now Advocacy Team
title: #NoExamShutdown: One step forward, another step back
content:
Every year, when exam season rolls around for students across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), many governments use the risk of cheating as an excuse to shut down the internet or block social media platforms. And every year, this results in millions of people losing connectivity, businesses grinding to a halt, and disruption to daily life across entire countries. Of course, exam shutdowns are not the only threat to education in the region; 

students in Gaza

 have begun a third academic year in tents and makeshift spaces, while in Lebanon, nearly 

100,000

 students were unable to return to school at all.




But across the wider MENA region, this year’s exam season saw mixed results for exam shutdowns. For the first time since Access Now, 

SMEX,

 and the 

Internet Society

 began tracking this phenomenon as part of the 

#NoExamShutdown campaign

, the trend went in two different directions across the map. For example, Algeria, which has been a persistent offender for the past decade, 

limited shutdown measures

 to the inside of exam centres, without disconnecting the rest of the country. Meanwhile Syria, which imposed 

11 nationwide exam-related shutdowns just last year

, appears to have held its 2026 exams without any documented disruptions. On the other hand, Tunisia — a country previously ranked as having the

author: Wajd
title: Urgent global call following the referral of Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah to trial
content:
Over a hundred civil society organizations and independent media outlets from around the world have come together to stand in solidarity with Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah following her referral to trial in Egypt.

We, the undersigned civil society organizations and independent media outlets from around the world, join together to condemn the unprecedented attack on press freedom in Egypt following the referral of Egyptian journalist and Editor-in-Chief of independent media outlet Mada Masr Lina Attalah to trial.

Just hours after Mada Masr joined seven other independent media outlets from across the Arab world in setting up a solidarity flash newsroom to fill the gap in coverage following the arrest of the entire newsroom of Egyptian investigative platform Matsadaash, on October 19, 2026, Lina Attalah received a summons to appear for questioning before the Supreme State Security Prosecution pending Case No. 9072 of 2026. The reasons for the summons were not disclosed.

At the interrogation, which took place on October 21 and lasted over six hours, Lina was questioned about Mada’s coverage on the wave of protests happening in prisons across the country, as well as the legal status of Mada Masr’s license. She was faced with charges of running a website without a license and of publishing false news with the aim of disturbing public peace and ultimately released on LE 10

author: Franco Giandana Gigena
title: Openness in AI development: a path to long-term independence
content:
As concerns grow over 

deepening dependencies

 on a handful of Big Tech companies and the 

outsized influence

 of the U.S. and China, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk used his speech during July’s inaugural 

Global Dialogue on AI Governance

 to call on humans to 

“take back our agency”

 over AI. But what does agency over AI really mean? What policies and practices can allow people to shape AI in ways that respect, rather than undermine, 

human rights

? 




This blog post unpacks concrete initiatives that show how openness in AI development can increase people’s agency over AI and advance the development of public interest technology. At the same time, we reflect on how openness is not the same thing as mere access, and how short-term pragmatism can pave the way toward long-term independence.

, intended to “advance scientific understanding and ensure that international deliberations are informed by the best available evidence.” The panel’s

author: Amina Khan
title: Beware of spyware: Access Now urges pension funds to scrutinize investments for spyware exposure
content:
On September 28, 2026, Access Now wrote to four pension funds — 

Los Angeles County Employees Retirement Association

, 

Houston Firefighters’ Relief and Retirement Fund

, 

New Mexico Educational Retirement Board

, and  

Hampshire Pension Fund

 — regarding their investment in AE Industrial Partners (AEI). AEI 

purchased

 spyware technology vendor Paragon Solutions in 2024 and merged the company with its holding company REDLattice. The letters urge pension fund managers to use their leverage with AEI to ensure the fund “provide[s] remedy where warranted, and implement robust safeguards” to prevent any contribution to human rights breaches.













Investors have a responsibility to identify and address human rights risks in their portfolios. Paragon presents a clear risk given its appalling human rights record, and these pension funds should avoid exposure to such spyware in their portfolios and demand answers from AE Industrial Partners.
